strengths: The manuscript addresses an identifiable audience studying classification with strong correlations and factor structure. Sparsity of the whitened mean difference offers an interesting alternative to sparsity of the raw discriminant direction. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b10/review-experiment-szuob3xs/call-92fc6979786c483cb72cf6a9b60e1e7a/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The decomposition into eigenspace estimation, coordinatewise estimation of the whitened direction, and support recovery provides a useful framework. Retaining information outside the leading principal-component subspace is also well motivated.

The algorithms and principal assumptions are explicitly presented, with substantial supplementary derivations. The experimental design includes several relevant baselines, 200 Monte Carlo replications, and held-out evaluations on two gene-expression datasets.
weaknesses: Necessary: The central consistency theorem is not established as stated. Theorem 3 asserts almost-sure convergence of conditional classification risk under log(p)=o(n), whereas Section 8.4 ends with joint score convergence in probability under the stronger condition log(n)log(p)=o(n). This does not establish the stated growth regime or almost-sure conditional-risk conclusion. Supply the missing argument or weaken the theorem and dependent claims, including Theorem 5. The abstract should also make clear that Assumption 2 requires uniformly bounded support size and nonvanishing minimum signal.

Necessary: The QDA extension contains a substantive mathematical error. Equation (5.9) drops coordinates outside the supports of the whitened means, although those coordinates can discriminate through covariance differences. For example, take equal priors, Σ₀=I+p uuᵀ with u=p^(-1/2)1, Σ₁=Σ₀, Σ₂=4Σ₀, μ₁=Σ₀^(1/2)e₁, and μ₂=2Σ₀^(1/2)e₁. Both whitened means equal e₁, satisfying the stated sparsity, signal, and coherence conditions. The proposed population reduction uses only one coordinate, whose best classification error is approximately 30.5%, while the full Bayes error tends to zero because the remaining coordinates distinguish variance 1 from variance 4 after transformation by Σ₀^(-1/2). Thus Theorem 6 is false under the stated conditions. Additional structural restrictions, a different reduction, or removal of this extension is necessary.

Necessary: Section 5.1 incorrectly treats Gaussian LDA as Bayes optimal for general elliptical distributions with unequal priors. For a common radial density h, the Bayes decision compares log h(q₁) and log h(q₂), including prior odds; this generally does not yield Equation (1.1). Sub-Gaussian tails do not resolve this issue, and bounded scale mixtures of Gaussians provide counterexamples. Restrict the claim to an appropriate setting, such as common radial densities with equal priors, or derive and analyze the correct decision rule. The corresponding elliptical multiclass claim also needs correction.

Necessary: The reported oracle results conflict with the stated simulation models. For Model 2, the squared Mahalanobis distance is [10−100ρ/(1+19ρ)]/(1−ρ). At ρ=0.9, Equation (3.1) therefore gives a Bayes error of approximately 0.0196%, whereas Table 3 reports 5.40%. This discrepancy is far beyond Monte Carlo uncertainty over 200 replications. Several entries in Table 1 are also repeated exactly between ρ=0.7 and ρ=0.8 despite changing model parameters. Audit the simulation specifications, implementations, and tables, and provide corrected evidence before relying on the comparative conclusions.

Necessary: The feature-count comparisons need narrower interpretation. The proposed method counts selected whitened coordinates, while several baselines count raw discriminant coefficients. A selected whitened coordinate generally depends on every original variable through a dense whitening matrix, so these counts do not establish fewer required measurements or a smaller overall model. Although Section 2 acknowledges the distinction, the conclusions should consistently describe sparsity in transformed coordinates. The imposed search range s≤30 also constrains the reported model sizes and should be considered when interpreting this advantage.

Necessary clarification: Section 2.3 defines Λ̂ as the leading eigenvalues of the sample covariance, but subsequently uses D̂=(Λ̂+σ̂²I)^(-1/2). Those sample eigenvalues already estimate λk+σ², so this adds the bulk variance twice relative to the population formula. Resolve the definition/formula inconsistency and specify which estimator produced the experiments. Also distinguish the theoretical treatment with known d from the practical 90%-explained-variance rule, which need not recover the spike count.

Optional improvements: After resolving these correctness issues, experiments varying sample size, dimension, spike strength, and tuning choices would help connect the asymptotic results to practice. More complete preprocessing details and proofreading would improve reproducibility and presentation. These additions are secondary; the rejection recommendation rests on unsupported or false claims and inconsistent numerical evidence, rather than insufficient novelty or impact.
